qadi.s: A qadi is a judge in Islamic law, responsible for applying sharia in civil, family and criminal cases. Qadis were appointed by Muslim rulers from the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates onwards.

qadiriyya.s: The Qadiriyya is one of the oldest and most widespread Sufi orders in Islam, named after the twelfth-century scholar Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate, belonged to the order.

qahtanites.s: The Qahtanites are the Arabs who traced their descent from the legendary ancestor Qahtan, associated with southern Arabia and Yemen. In the Umayyad period the Yemeni or Qahtani tribal faction was bitterly opposed to the northern Arab Qays.

qajar-capture-of-shiraz.s: The Qajar capture of Shiraz was the taking of the Zand capital by Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar in 1791. According to the site it completed the formal dissolution of the Zand Empire.

qajar-dynasty.s: The Qajar dynasty was a Turkmen dynasty that ruled Iran from the late eighteenth century until 1925. Its founder Agha Mohammad Khan defeated the Zand Empire and in 1796 took Mashhad, ending the last remnant of the Afsharid Empire.

qalawun.s: Qalawun was a sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate in the late thirteenth century and founder of a dynasty that ruled for about a century. His campaigns continued the work of Baybars against the Crusader states and the Mongols.

qanat.s: A qanat is an underground channel that carries water by gravity from mountain aquifers to lowland fields and settlements. The technique originated in ancient Iran and spread across arid regions.

qapaghan-qaghan.s: Qapaghan Qaghan was a ruler of the Second Turkic Khaganate from 691 to 716. He was its leading military commander, crossing the Yellow River repeatedly to force tribute from the Tang and conquering the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 710.

qara-khitai.s: The Qara Khitai, or Western Liao, was a Central Asian state founded in the twelfth century by Khitan refugees from northern China after the fall of the Liao dynasty. It defeated the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141, destroying Seljuk Empire authority…

qarmatians.s: The Qarmatians were a radical Ismaili movement based mainly in eastern Arabia and Bahrain from the late ninth century. They raided widely and famously seized the Black Stone from Mecca in 930.

qarshi.s: Qarshi is a city in southern Uzbekistan, in the region of Transoxiana. In the 1320s Kebek Khan of the Chagatai Empire attempted to make it a stable sedentary capital.

qays.s: The Qays were the northern Arab tribal grouping that opposed the Yemeni or Qahtani faction in the early Islamic period. Their rivalry dominated the politics and armies of the late Umayyad period.

qazi.s: Qazi is the form of the Arabic word qadi, meaning a judge in Islamic law, used in Persian and South Asian contexts. In the Delhi Sultanate qazi courts administered sharia as the formal legal framework of the state.

qianlong-emperor.s: The Qianlong Emperor ruled the Qing Empire from 1735 to 1796, presiding over its greatest territorial extent. His Ten Great Campaigns conquered Dzungaria and Eastern Turkestan and reached into Burma, Vietnam and Nepal.

qin-dynasty.s: The Qin dynasty was the first imperial dynasty of China, which unified the country in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang. It standardised writing, weights and measures and created a centralised bureaucratic state.

qing-conquest-of-taiwan.s: The Qing conquest of Taiwan took place in 1683, when Qing naval forces under Shi Lang defeated the Kingdom of Tungning ruled by the descendants of Koxinga. The island had been the last stronghold of Ming loyalist resistance.

qing-empire.s: The Qing Empire was the last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus, who conquered Ming China from 1644 and ruled until 1912. It expanded China's territory to include Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet and presided over great population and commercial growth.

qiniq.s: The Qiniq were a clan of the Oghuz Turks of Central Asia. Seljuk Beg, the eponymous ancestor of the Seljuk dynasty, was a chieftain of the Qiniq who converted to Sunni Islam around 985 CE.

qizilbash.s: The Qizilbash were a confederation of Turkmen tribes devoted to the Safavid Sufi order, named after their distinctive red headgear. They brought Ismail I to power in 1501 and formed the core military and political elite of the Safavid Empire.

quanzhou.s: Quanzhou is a port city in Fujian province in south-eastern China. Under the Song Dynasty it was one of the busiest ports in the world, linking China with South-east Asia, India, the Persian Gulf and East Africa.

quchan.s: Quchan is a town in Khorasan in north-eastern Iran. Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid Empire, was assassinated by his own officers near Quchan on 20 June 1747.

quebec.s: Quebec is a city on the St Lawrence River in Canada. Samuel de Champlain founded it in 1608 as the capital of New France and the centre of the fur trade.

queen-of-sheba.s: The Queen of Sheba is a figure from biblical and Quranic tradition who visited King Solomon. Ethiopian tradition, codified in the Kebra Nagast, holds that she bore Solomon a son, Menelik, founder of a royal line.

quelimane.s: Quelimane is a port town on the coast of Mozambique, near the Zambezi delta. In the eighteenth century gold and ivory from the Zimbabwean plateau reached the coast through Quelimane and Sofala.

quinquereme.s: A quinquereme was a large ancient warship powered by oarsmen arranged in groups of five per vertical unit. It was the standard battleship of the Hellenistic and Punic navies.

quintus-fabius-maximus.s: Quintus Fabius Maximus was a Roman statesman and general during the Second Punic War. After Hannibal's early victories he adopted a strategy of avoiding pitched battle and wearing down the Carthaginian army, earning the name Cunctator, the delayer.

quran.s: The Quran is the central religious text of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. Under the caliph Uthman of the Rashidun Caliphate its text was standardised into a single authoritative recension.

quraysh.s: The Quraysh were the dominant Arab tribe of Mecca, to which the Prophet Muhammad belonged. Its Umayyad clan initially opposed Muhammad before his victory in 630 CE.

qurchi-bashi.s: The qurchi-bashi was the commander of the qurchis, the royal guard of Qizilbash cavalry, in the Safavid Empire. The office was one of the most powerful in the central administration, commanding the Qizilbash military establishment.

qut.s: Qut is an Old Turkic concept of heavenly charisma or good fortune, believed to be granted by the sky god Tengri to a legitimate ruler. Possession of qut justified a qaghan's authority over the steppe peoples.

qutb-minar.s: The Qutb Minar is a tall minaret of red sandstone in Delhi, begun around the end of the twelfth century under Qutb ud-Din Aibak and completed by his successors. It stands within a complex that includes one of the earliest mosques in India.

qutb-ud-din-aibak.s: Qutb ud-Din Aibak was a Turkic slave-general of the Ghurid ruler Muhammad of Ghor, who governed Delhi as viceroy from 1192. After his master's death he declared himself independent ruler, founding the Mamluk or Slave Dynasty.

qutuz.s: Qutuz was a sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate in 1259–1260. With the general Baybars he led the Mamluk army that defeated a Mongol force under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut in Galilee in 1260.

qutayba-ibn-muslim.s: Qutayba ibn Muslim was an Arab general and Umayyad governor of Khurasan from 705, appointed by al-Hajjaj. In a decade of campaigns he subdued Tokharistan, took Bukhara in 709 and Khwarazm and Samarkand in 712, and raided into Ferghana, bringing Transoxiana under Muslim rule.

qara-yusuf.s: Qara Yusuf was the leader of the Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen confederation from 1388 to 1420. Driven out by Timur, he returned after Timur's death, killed the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad in 1410 and took Tabriz and Baghdad, making the Qara Qoyunlu the leading power in Azerbaijan and Iraq.

quintus-caecilius-metellus-creticus.s: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus was a Roman general and consul in 69 BCE. Sent against the Cretan cities, which Rome accused of aiding pirates, he besieged Kydonia, Knossos and other towns between 69 and 67 BCE and conquered the whole island.

quintus-caecilius-metellus-macedonicus.s: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus was a Roman general and statesman. As praetor in 148 BCE he defeated Andriscus, the pretender who had briefly revived the Macedonian monarchy, ending the Fourth Macedonian War.

quintus-caecilius-metellus-balearicus.s: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Balearicus was a Roman consul of 123 BCE who conquered the Balearic Islands, whose people were accused of harbouring pirates. He settled Roman colonists from Iberia there and founded the towns of Palma and Pollentia on Mallorca, earning the surname…

qiao-zong.s: Qiao Zong was an official who rebelled against the Eastern Jin in Sichuan in 405 and founded the state of Western Shu, ruling from Chengdu. He accepted titles from Later Qin and tried to expand down the Yangtze.

quang-trung.s: Quang Trung, born Nguyen Hue, was the ablest of the three Tay Son brothers who rose against the Nguyen lords in 1771. He overthrew the Trinh lords in 1786, proclaimed himself emperor in 1788 and routed a Qing invasion at Dong Da in 1789.

qalat-al-bahrain.s: Qal'at al-Bahrain is an archaeological site on the north coast of Bahrain, occupied from about 2300 BCE to the 18th century. It was a walled town and probably the capital of Dilmun, and later the site of a fort rebuilt by the Portuguese in the 16th century.

qara-yuluk-osman.s: Qara Yuluk Osman was the chief of the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen confederation around Diyarbakir. In 1398 he killed Kadi Burhan al-Din of Sivas.

qazi-muhammad.s: Qazi Muhammad was a Kurdish judge and religious leader of Mahabad who led the Kurdistan Democratic Party and became president of the Soviet-backed Republic of Mahabad, proclaimed in January 1946. When Soviet troops left Iran, Iranian forces reoccupied Mahabad, and he was…

qu-wentai.s: Qu Wentai was king of Gaochang, the oasis kingdom of Turpan on the Silk Road, from 620. A devout Buddhist, he welcomed the monk Xuanzang in 630 and funded his journey to India.

queen-victoria.s: Victoria was queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901 and empress of India from 1876. Her long reign saw industrial growth, political reform and the expansion of the British Empire.

quintus-poppaedius-silo.s: Quintus Poppaedius Silo was a leader of the Marsi and one of the two consuls of the Italian confederation of Italia in the Social War against Rome, which began in 91 BCE. He was the most capable of the rebel commanders and won several victories, but he was killed in battle in…

quintus-titurius-sabinus.s: Quintus Titurius Sabinus was a legate of Julius Caesar in the Gallic Wars. In 56 BCE he routed the coalition of the Unelli, Lexovii and Aulerci Eburovices under Viridovix by luring them to attack his hilltop camp.

qin-shi-huang.s: Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, became king of the State of Qin in 246 BCE and between 230 and 221 BCE conquered the six rival Warring States, unifying China. He took the new title Huangdi, emperor, and is known as the First Emperor.

qutb-ud-din-mubarak-shah.s: Qutb ud-Din Mubarak Shah was the last sultan of the Khalji dynasty of Delhi, ruling from 1316 to 1320 after the death of his father Alauddin Khalji. In 1317–1318 he led an army to the Deccan, crushed the revolt of the Yadava prince Harapala Deva and annexed the Seuna kingdom…

quintus-petillius-cerialis.s: Quintus Petillius Cerialis was a Roman general and governor of Britain from 71 to 74 CE. As a legionary commander he had been defeated during Boudica's revolt, and in 70 he put down the Batavian revolt on the Rhine.

qaboos-bin-said.s: Qaboos bin Said was sultan of Oman from 1970 to 2020, the longest-serving ruler in the Arab world at his death. He deposed his father Said bin Taimur, renamed the country the Sultanate of Oman, defeated the Dhofar rebellion and used oil revenue to build roads, schools and…

qahtan-al-shaabi.s: Qahtan al-Shaabi was a leader of the National Liberation Front who became the first president of South Yemen when Britain withdrew from Aden on 30 November 1967. He abolished the sultanates of the former Aden Protectorate, but in June 1969 the party's left wing removed him,…

qakare-ibi.s: Qakare Ibi was a king of Egypt's Eighth Dynasty in the First Intermediate Period, known from the Abydos king list. His small pyramid at South Saqqara, the only identified royal pyramid of that dynasty, is inscribed with Pyramid Texts, showing that Old Kingdom royal traditions…

qasim-barid.s: Qasim Barid was a Turkic noble who became chief minister of the declining Bahmani Sultanate in the 1490s and controlled its last sultans from Bidar. He founded the Barid Shahi dynasty, and his son Amir Barid continued to rule in the Bahmanis' name before his descendants took…

qasim-khan-of-qasim.s: Qasim Khan was a son of Ulugh Muhammad, founder of the Kazan Khanate, who entered the service of Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow. Around 1452 he received the town of Gorodets Meshchersky on the Oka, later named Kasimov after him, as the seat of a Tatar vassal khanate that…

qasr-ibrim.s: Qasr Ibrim is a fortified hilltop site in Lower Nubia, now an island in Lake Nasser, occupied for some three thousand years until the early 19th century. It was a temple town, a Roman outpost, a seat of Blemmye and Nobadian power and later a Christian cathedral town of Makuria.

qatada-ibn-idris.s: Qatada ibn Idris was a Hasanid sharif from Yanbu who took Mecca in 1201 and founded the line of the Banu Qatada. His descendants ruled Mecca as sharifs under the successive powers of Egypt and later the Ottomans until 1925, when the Hashemite kingdom of the Hejaz fell to Ibn…

qavam-al-din-marashi.s: Qavam al-Din Mar'ashi, known as Mir-i Buzurg, was a Twelver Shia sayyid and Sufi teacher in Mazandaran whose dervish followers became a political force. In 1359 they defeated and killed Afrasiyab, ruler of Amol, and Qavam al-Din founded the Mar'ashi dynasty, which ruled…

qazaghan.s: Qazaghan was a Turkic amir of the Qara'unas who defeated and killed the Chagatai khan Qazan in 1346 or 1347 and became the real ruler of the western Chagatai Khanate in Transoxiana, governing through puppet khans. He was murdered in 1358.

qian-chu.s: Qian Chu was the last king of Wuyue, the coastal kingdom around Hangzhou, reigning from 947 to 978. He helped the Song dynasty conquer Southern Tang and in 978 handed his entire kingdom to Song without a fight, so that Wuyue's lands were spared war.

qian-liu.s: Qian Liu was the founder of Wuyue, one of the Ten Kingdoms of China. A former salt smuggler turned soldier, he gained control of the Zhejiang coast in the 890s, and in 907 the Later Liang made him king of Wuyue.

qifu-gangui.s: Qifu Gangui was the second ruler of Western Qin, a Xianbei state in Gansu during the Sixteen Kingdoms period. He succeeded his brother Qifu Guoren in 388, submitted to Later Qin in 400 and restored his state in 409.

qifu-guoren.s: Qifu Guoren was a chief of the Qifu clan of the Xianbei who founded Western Qin in 385, after the collapse of Former Qin following the Battle of Fei River. He ruled from Yuanchuan near modern Yuzhong in Gansu over Xianbei herders and Chinese farmers, and was succeeded by his…

qilian-mountains.s: The Qilian Mountains are a range on the north-eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, along the border of Gansu and Qinghai in China. Their snowmelt waters the oases of the Hexi Corridor, the route of the Silk Road between China and Central Asia.

qinghai-lake.s: Qinghai Lake, also known by its Mongolian name Kokonor, is the largest lake in China, a salt lake on the north-eastern Tibetan Plateau. Its grasslands supported pastoral peoples for millennia, and from the 4th to the 7th century they were the heartland of the Tuyuhun kingdom,…

qizil-arslan.s: Qizil Arslan was an atabeg of the Eldiguzid dynasty of Azerbaijan, the son of Eldiguz, who succeeded his brother Jahan Pahlavan in 1186. He fought the last Seljuk sultan Toghrul III, imprisoned him and proclaimed himself sultan, but was murdered in 1191.

quanah-parker.s: Quanah Parker was a war leader of the Kwahadi Comanche, the son of Peta Nocona and the captive Cynthia Ann Parker. After the Red River War he led the last free Comanche band to surrender at Fort Sill in 1875.

queau-de-quinssy.s: Jean-Baptiste Quéau de Quinssy was the French commandant of the Seychelles from 1794. During the Napoleonic Wars he surrendered the islands to British warships several times, negotiating terms that protected the settlers, and continued to govern.

quemuenchatocha.s: Quemuenchatocha was the zaque, ruler of the northern Muisca at Hunza (modern Tunja), when the Spanish arrived. In 1537 the conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada seized Hunza, captured the aged ruler and plundered his treasure.

quintus-opimius.s: Quintus Opimius was a Roman consul of 154 BCE. When the Ligurian Oxybii and Deciates attacked the Massalian towns of Antipolis and Nikaia, he led an army against them, took Aegitna and defeated both peoples, giving part of their land to Massalia.

quintus-sertorius.s: Quintus Sertorius was a Roman general of the Marian faction who, after Sulla's victory, made Hispania his base. With Lusitanian and Celtiberian allies he defeated the Senate's commanders Metellus Pius and Pompey for years, setting up his own senate and a school for Iberian…

qusayy-ibn-kilab.s: Qusayy ibn Kilab was, according to Arab tradition, the leader who gathered the scattered clans of the Quraysh in Mecca in the 5th century and won control of the Kaaba from the Khuza'a. He organised the pilgrimage and founded the Dar al-Nadwa, the council house of Mecca.

qutb-al-din-mawdud.s: Qutb al-Din Mawdud was the Zengid ruler of Mosul from 1149 to 1170, a son of Zengi and brother of Nur al-Din of Aleppo and Damascus. He generally supported his brother's campaigns against the Crusaders and governed Mosul and the Jazira, where his court patronised learning and…

qutb-ud-din-khan-of-kasur.s: Qutb-ud-din Khan was a Pathan ruler of Kasur in the Punjab in the early 19th century. After Ranjit Singh annexed Kasur around 1807, he received the lands of Mamdot on the south bank of the Sutlej in compensation, and his descendants ruled there as Nawabs of Mamdot, later under…

qutlugh-bilge-kol-qaghan.s: Qutlugh Bilge Kol Qaghan was the founder of the Uyghur Khaganate. In 744, as chief of the Uyghurs, he joined the Basmyls and Karluks to overthrow the Second Turkic Khaganate, then turned on his allies and became master of the Mongolian steppe.

qutlugh-terken-khatun.s: Qutlugh Terken Khatun was ruler of Kerman in southern Iran from 1257 to 1282, the widow of the Qutlugh-Khanid ruler Qutb al-Din Muhammad. Governing as a vassal of the Ilkhanate, she was remembered for justice, irrigation works and building.

quli-qutb-mulk.s: Quli Qutb Mulk, known as Sultan Quli, was a Turkmen noble from Hamadan who became governor of Telangana for the Bahmani Sultanate. As Bahmani power collapsed he became independent in 1518, founding the Qutb Shahi dynasty and the Golconda Sultanate, and fortified Golconda.

qerri.s: Qerri was a town on the Nile in Sudan, north of the confluence of the Blue and White Niles. From the early 16th century it was the seat of the Abdallab sheikhs, descendants of Abdallah Jamma, who governed the northern part of the Funj Sultanate of Sennar as its vassals.

qustul.s: Qustul is an archaeological site in Lower Nubia, on the Nile near the modern border between Egypt and Sudan, now under Lake Nasser. Its Cemetery L held large A-Group tombs of the late 4th millennium BCE with Egyptian goods, including an incense burner with royal imagery that…

qalacholan.s: Qalacholan was the early capital of the Baban emirate, a Kurdish principality in the Sharazur region of present-day Iraqi Kurdistan. In 1784 the Baban ruler Ibrahim Pasha moved his seat to the new town of Sulaymaniyah, named after the Ottoman governor of Baghdad, and…

quintus-fulvius-nobilior.s: Quintus Fulvius Nobilior was a Roman consul in 153 BCE, the year when consuls first took office on 1 January so that he could leave early for the war in Hispania. He was ambushed by the Celtiberians under Carus of Segeda and lost thousands of men, and his later assault on…

qudsia-begum.s: Qudsia Begum was the first of the four women rulers of Bhopal State. After her husband, Nawab Nazar Muhammad Khan, died in 1819, she governed as regent until 1837 despite opposition from male relatives.

quit-india-movement.s: The Quit India Movement was a mass campaign launched by the Indian National Congress on 8 August 1942, demanding an immediate end to British rule. The British arrested Gandhi and the Congress leadership at once, and the protests, strikes and sabotage that followed were…

quakers.s: The Quakers, or Religious Society of Friends, are a Christian movement founded by George Fox in England in the 1650s. They reject clergy and formal sacraments and meet in silent worship, waiting for the 'inner light'.

qabala.s: Qabala is a town in northern Azerbaijan on the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus. Near it lie the ruins of ancient Kabala, the early capital of Caucasian Albania, mentioned by Pliny and Ptolemy, with walls and gates excavated by archaeologists.

quang-binh-province.s: Quảng Bình is a historical province of north-central Vietnam, merged into Quảng Trị province in 2025. It marked the northern edge of Champa's coastal lands until the Vietnamese gained the area in the 11th century, and in the 17th and 18th centuries the Nguyễn lords defended it…

quetzalcoatl.s: Quetzalcoatl, "feathered serpent", is a Mesoamerican deity associated with wind, learning, priesthood and the morning star. Images of a feathered serpent appear at Teotihuacan by the 3rd century CE, and the god was later linked with the legendary Toltec priest-king Topiltzin…

quimper.s: Quimper is a city in Finistère, western Brittany, at the confluence of the Odet and Steir rivers, and the historic capital of Cornouaille. It grew around the see traditionally founded by Saint Corentin, whose Gothic cathedral dominates the town, and its counts became dukes of…

querfurt.s: Querfurt is a town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, west of Halle, dominated by one of the largest medieval castles in Germany. It was the seat of the lords of Querfurt, whose family included the missionary Bruno of Querfurt and who took over the Mansfeld lands in 1229.

quercy.s: Quercy is a historic province of south-western France around Cahors, roughly the modern department of Lot and part of Tarn-et-Garonne. In the Middle Ages it was contested between the counts of Toulouse, the dukes of Aquitaine and the French crown, and it suffered heavily in…

qianan.s: Qian'an is a county-level city in Tangshan prefecture, north-eastern Hebei province, China, on the Luan River near the Great Wall. In the late 3rd and early 4th centuries the area was the base of the Duan Xianbei, whose seat at Lingzhi lay nearby.

qimin-khagan.s: Qimin Khagan was a ruler of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate from 599 to 609. A prince who had lost out in the Turkic civil wars, he took refuge with the Sui dynasty, married a Sui princess and was installed as khagan with Chinese support.

quanrong.s: The Quanrong were a people living on the western and north-western borders of the Zhou realm in early China, counted by Zhou writers among the non-Chinese Rong. In 771 BCE, allied with the Marquis of Shen, they sacked the Western Zhou capital Haojing and killed King You.

quintipartite-deed.s: The Quintipartite Deed of 1 July 1676 divided the English colony of New Jersey into East Jersey and West Jersey. It was signed by Sir George Carteret and by the trustees of the Quaker proprietor Edward Byllynge, including William Penn, and set a dividing line from Little Egg…

qaus-gabri.s: Qaus-gabri was a king of Edom in the early 7th century BCE, known from Assyrian records. He appears among the western vassal kings who sent building materials to Esarhaddon for his palace at Nineveh and who supported Ashurbanipal's campaign against Egypt.

qos.s: Qos was the national god of the Edomites, worshipped in the Iron Age in the lands south-east of the Dead Sea. His name appears in Edomite royal names such as Qaus-gabri and Qaus-malaku, and his cult continued among the Idumaeans into the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

qudshanis.s: Qudshanis is a village in Hakkâri Province in south-eastern Turkey. From the 17th century until the First World War it was the seat of the Shimun line of patriarchs of the Church of the East, who led the Assyrian Christian tribes of the Hakkari mountains.

quadragesimo-anno.s: Quadragesimo Anno is an encyclical issued by Pope Pius XI on 15 May 1931, forty years after Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum. Written during the Great Depression, it criticised both unrestrained capitalism and socialism, set out the principle of subsidiarity, and proposed reorganising…

qutb-shahi-dynasty.s: The Qutb Shahi dynasty ruled the Golconda Sultanate in the Deccan from 1518 to 1687. Founded by Sultan Quli, a Turkmen officer of the Bahmani Sultanate, these Shia rulers grew rich on diamonds and textiles, founded Hyderabad in 1591 and patronised Telugu, Persian and Dakhni…

qalat-beni-hammad.s: Qal'at Beni Hammad is the ruined first capital of the Hammadid dynasty, in the Hodna Mountains of north-central Algeria, founded around 1007 by Hammad ibn Buluggin. It grew into a city of palaces, mosques and workshops, whose great minaret still stands, and was famed for its…

qena.s: Qena is a city in Upper Egypt on the east bank of the Nile, capital of Qena Governorate and close to the temple of Dendera. It stands where the shortest route from the Nile to the Red Sea leaves the valley and was long a centre of trade and pilgrim traffic.

quedlinburg.s: Quedlinburg is a town on the northern edge of the Harz in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. A favoured residence of the Ottonian kings, it was the burial place of Henry the Fowler, whose widow Matilda founded an abbey of noble canonesses there in 936; its abbesses ruled the town as…

qhapaq-nan.s: The Qhapaq Ñan was the road network of the Inca Empire, some 40,000 kilometres long, running along the Andes and the Pacific coast from present-day Colombia to Chile and Argentina. Way stations called tambos and relay runners called chaskis allowed armies, officials and…

quechua.s: Quechua is a family of languages spoken by some eight to ten million people in the Andes, chiefly in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador. The Incas used it as the administrative language of their empire, and Spanish missionaries promoted it as a common language for preaching.

queen-shima.s: Queen Shima was a ruler of Holing, or Kalingga, on the north coast of Java, said in the New Book of Tang to have been chosen as ruler in 674. Chinese and Javanese tradition remembers her for strict justice: a bag of gold left on the road lay untouched for years until her own…

qashliq.s: Qashliq, also called Isker, was the capital of the Khanate of Sibir, on the right bank of the Irtysh near modern Tobolsk in western Siberia. The Taibugid rulers made it their seat around 1495, and in 1582 the Cossacks of Yermak took it from Khan Kuchum.

quetzaltenango.s: Quetzaltenango, called Xelajú or Xela, is the second-largest city of Guatemala, in the western highlands. Near it Pedro de Alvarado defeated the K'iche' in 1524, and it became a Spanish town.

qumarkaj.s: Q'umarkaj, called Utatlán by the Spanish, was the capital of the K'iche' Maya kingdom in the highlands of Guatemala, near modern Santa Cruz del Quiché. Founded in the 15th century on a plateau protected by ravines, it held temples, palaces and a ballcourt.

qana-yemen.s: Qana was the main port of the ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt, on the Arabian Sea coast of southern Yemen near modern Bir Ali. Frankincense from Dhofar and the interior was collected there for shipment, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes it in the 1st century CE.

quintana-roo.s: Quintana Roo is a state of Mexico on the eastern side of the Yucatán Peninsula, along the Caribbean coast. It holds Maya sites such as Tulum, Cobá and Dzibanche, and was long a stronghold of rebel Maya during the Caste War.

qaryat-al-faw.s: Qaryat al-Faw is an archaeological site in south-western Saudi Arabia, on the north-western edge of the Rub' al Khali (Empty Quarter). From about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE it was a caravan town on the incense route, and it is identified with Qaryat Dhat Kahl,…

qarnawu.s: Qarnawu was the capital of the ancient South Arabian Kingdom of Ma'in, in the al-Jawf valley of northern Yemen. Its walled ruins, at the modern site of Ma'in, contain gates and temples, and Minaic inscriptions name it as the seat of the kings.

qalhat.s: Qalhat is an ancient port city on the coast of Oman, south of Sur. From the 11th to the 15th century it was the second city of the kingdom of Hormuz and a major trading port of the Arabian Sea, described by Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.

qatabanian-language.s: Qatabanian is an Old South Arabian language spoken in the ancient kingdom of Qataban in Yemen and written in the South Arabian script. It is known from several hundred inscriptions of roughly the 5th century BCE to the 2nd century CE, including royal decrees, dedications and…

queen-amina.s: Amina is remembered in Hausa tradition as a warrior queen of Zazzau, in present-day northern Nigeria, usually placed in the 16th century. The Kano Chronicle says that she conquered lands as far as Nupe and Kwararafa and that tribute came to her from many towns.

quintus-pleminius.s: Quintus Pleminius was a Roman officer whom Scipio Africanus left in command of Locri after its recapture from Hannibal in 205 BCE. He and his troops plundered the town and the treasury of its sanctuary of Persephone, and he had two military tribunes flogged to death.

qishn.s: Qishn is a coastal town in Al Mahrah Governorate in eastern Yemen, on the Arabian Sea. It was the mainland seat of the Mahra Sultanate of Qishn and Socotra, ruled by the Afrar family, until the sultanate was abolished in 1967 and absorbed into South Yemen.

qalaichi.s: Qalaichi is an archaeological site near Bukan in West Azerbaijan province, north-western Iran, linked with the Mannaean kingdom of the early 1st millennium BCE. Excavations found a fortified building decorated with glazed bricks and fragments of an Aramaic stele of the 8th…

qumbu.s: Qumbu is a small town in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa, between Mthatha and Mount Frere. It lies in the former lands of the Mpondomise kingdom and became a magistracy after Cape annexation.

quintus-tullius-cicero.s: Quintus Tullius Cicero was a Roman politician and soldier, the younger brother of the orator Marcus Tullius Cicero. As one of Julius Caesar's legates in Gaul, in 54 BCE he held his winter camp in the territory of the Nervii against a prolonged siege until Caesar relieved him.

qadmus.s: Qadmus is a town in the coastal mountains of western Syria, in Tartus governorate, built around a medieval castle. The Nizari Ismailis acquired the castle in 1132, the first of the fortresses they gained in the mountains of the Jabal Bahra, and it remained one of their…

quhistan.s: Quhistan, or Kuhistan, 'land of mountains', is a historical region of eastern Iran south of Khorasan, around the towns of Qa'in, Tun and Birjand. From the 1090s it was one of the main territories of the Nizari Ismaili state, with many fortresses under a chief appointed from…

qaqortoq.s: Qaqortoq, formerly Julianehåb, is the largest town in southern Greenland, founded as a Danish trading post in 1775. It lies in the area of the medieval Norse Eastern Settlement, whose best-preserved ruin, Hvalsey Church, is nearby.

qarawiyyin-mosque.s: The Qarawiyyin Mosque is a mosque and centre of learning in Fez, Morocco, founded in 857 or 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a merchant from Kairouan. Greatly enlarged under the Almoravids in the 1130s and 1140s, when much of its present decoration was added, it became…

qadi-isa-savaji.s: Qadi Isa Savaji was a judge and leading minister of the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Ya'qub (r. 1478–1490). He attempted a fiscal reform that aimed to revoke hereditary tax exemptions, known as soyurghal, and to bring taxation closer to Islamic law.

qutlu-beg.s: Qutlu Beg was a chief of the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen tribes of eastern Anatolia in the fourteenth century, son of Tur Ali Beg and father of Qara Yuluk Osman. In 1352 he married Maria Komnene, sister of Emperor Alexios III of Trebizond, beginning a long series of marriage alliances…

quintus-marcius-philippus.s: Quintus Marcius Philippus was a Roman politician who was consul in 186 BCE and again in 169 BCE. Sent as an envoy to Greece in 172–171 BCE, he gained time for Rome by negotiating a truce with Perseus of Macedon and persuaded the Boeotian cities to abandon their league.

qadi-abd-al-jabbar.s: Qadi Abd al-Jabbar was a leading Mu'tazili theologian and jurist who served as chief judge at Ray under the Buyids, appointed through the vizier al-Sahib ibn Abbad. His vast work al-Mughni is the fullest surviving statement of Mu'tazili theology, covering God's unity and…

qabus.s: Qabus ibn Wushmgir was a ruler of the Ziyarid dynasty of Gurgan and Tabaristan, reigning from 977 to 981 and again from 997 to 1012. Driven out by the Buyids for sheltering Fakhr al-Dawla, he spent years in exile among the Samanids before recovering his lands.

quiet-revolution.s: The Quiet Revolution was the rapid secularisation and modernisation of Quebec in the 1960s, beginning with the election of Jean Lesage's Liberal government in 1960. The province took over education and social services from the Catholic Church, nationalised hydroelectric…

quintus-caecilius-metellus-pius.s: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius was a Roman general and politician, a supporter of Sulla and consul with him in 80 BCE. As governor of Hispania Ulterior from 79 BCE he fought the rebel Quintus Sertorius for most of a decade, later alongside Pompey, until the war ended in 72 BCE.

quintus-fulvius-flaccus-consul-179-bce.s: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus was a Roman general and politician who, as praetor in Hispania Citerior from 182 to 180 BCE, fought hard campaigns against the Celtiberians in the First Celtiberian War. He was consul in 179 BCE and censor in 174 BCE, when he controversially took marble…

quintus-pompeius-consul-141-bce.s: Quintus Pompeius was a Roman politician, the first of his family to reach the consulship, in 141 BCE. Succeeding Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus in Hispania Citerior, he failed to take Numantia and Termantia and made a secret peace with the Numantines, which he then…

qaraunas.s: The Qara'unas were a Turco-Mongol military people of the borderlands of Afghanistan and Khurasan, descended from Mongol garrison troops stationed there in the thirteenth century. They became one of the leading tribal groupings of the Chagatai Khanate, and their amir Qazaghan…

qutlugh-khwaja.s: Qutlugh Khwaja was a Chagataid prince, a son of Duwa, who commanded the Chagatai forces in Afghanistan and led raids into the Delhi Sultanate. In 1299 he led a large army to Kili on the outskirts of Delhi, where Alauddin Khalji met him in battle.

quwwat-ul-islam-mosque.s: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque is the earliest surviving mosque in Delhi, begun in the 1190s by Qutb al-Din Aybak after the Ghurid conquest, in what is now the Qutb complex. It was built largely of columns and stones taken from demolished Hindu and Jain temples, with a great…

qasim-razvi.s: Qasim Razvi was the leader of the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen in Hyderabad State from 1946 and commander of its Razakar militia, which resisted accession to India and attacked opponents and villages. After the Indian army annexed Hyderabad in 1948 he was imprisoned.

quizquiz.s: Quizquiz was one of the leading generals of the Inca ruler Atahualpa. With Chalcuchímac he defeated and captured Atahualpa's brother Huáscar near Cusco in 1532.

quanzhen-school.s: The Quanzhen (Complete Perfection) School is a branch of Daoism founded by Wang Chongyang in northern China under the Jin dynasty in the 1160s. Drawing on Buddhism and Confucianism, it stressed celibacy, monastic life, meditation and inner alchemy.

qvarqvare-ii-jaqeli.s: Qvarqvare II Jaqeli was atabeg of Samtskhe, a principality in south-western Georgia, from 1451 to 1498. Seeking independence from the Georgian crown, he captured King George VIII in 1465, which helped bring about the break-up of the united Kingdom of Georgia.

quintus-curtius-rufus.s: Quintus Curtius Rufus was a Roman historian, probably of the 1st century CE, author of the Histories of Alexander the Great in ten books, of which the first two are lost. Drawing on earlier Greek sources, his work is one of the main surviving accounts of Alexander's campaigns…

quentovic.s: Quentovic was a Frankish trading port near the mouth of the river Canche, close to modern Étaples in northern France, active from the seventh to the ninth century. With Dorestad it was one of the main emporia linking the Frankish lands with England, and it had a royal toll…

qansuh-al-ghawri.s: Qansuh al-Ghawri was the penultimate Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria, reigning from 1501 to 1516. He built a fleet to fight the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean, which was defeated at the Battle of Diu in 1509, and left a large mosque and mausoleum complex in Cairo.

qaitbay.s: Qaitbay was Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria from 1468 to 1496, one of the longest and most stable reigns of the Circassian period. He fought the Ottomans to a standstill in a war of 1485–1491 and was a great builder, leaving his funerary complex in Cairo's Northern Cemetery…

quitzow-family.s: The Quitzow family was a noble family of the Prignitz in Brandenburg. During the weak rule of the Luxembourg margraves around 1400, the brothers Dietrich and Johann von Quitzow dominated much of the Mark through feuds and the seizure of castles.

qi-jiguang.s: Qi Jiguang was a Ming dynasty general who defeated the wokou pirates raiding the coasts of Zhejiang and Fujian in the 1550s and 1560s. He trained disciplined volunteer armies in small-unit tactics such as the 'mandarin duck' formation and wrote military manuals, including the…

quebec-act.s: The Quebec Act was a British law of 1774 for the government of the Province of Quebec. It guaranteed free practice of the Catholic faith, restored French civil law while keeping English criminal law, and extended the province to the Ohio valley and the Great Lakes.

quintus-caecilius-metellus-numidicus.s: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus was a Roman general and leading conservative politician. As consul in 109 BCE he took command against Jugurtha, restored discipline and defeated him at the Muthul, but he was replaced by his former officer Gaius Marius in 107 BCE.

qeqchi-people.s: The Q'eqchi' are a Maya people of Guatemala and Belize, centred on the department of Alta Verapaz and spreading into Izabal, the Petén and southern Belize. Their language, Q'eqchi', is one of the most widely spoken Mayan languages, with more than a million speakers.

quintus-lollius-urbicus.s: Quintus Lollius Urbicus was a Roman general from Numidia in North Africa who served as governor of Britain from about 139 to 142 under Antoninus Pius. He reoccupied southern Scotland and built the Antonine Wall between the Forth and the Clyde, moving the frontier north of…

qin-zhong.s: Qin Zhong was a leader of the Qin people in the ninth century BCE, ruling from about 844 to 822 BCE. King Xuan of Zhou made him a grandee and charged him with fighting the Western Rong, against whom the Qin defended the Zhou frontier.

qutalmish.s: Qutalmish was a Seljuk prince, a cousin of Sultan Tughril, who took part in the Seljuk conquests in Iran and Iraq in the mid-eleventh century. He contested the succession after Tughril's death and died in 1064 fighting Sultan Alp Arslan.

qusayr-amra.s: Qusayr Amra is a small Umayyad desert palace and bath-house in eastern Jordan, built in the early eighth century, probably for the prince al-Walid ibn Yazid, later the caliph al-Walid II, between about 723 and 743. Its walls carry the largest surviving cycle of early Islamic…

qatar-and-dubai-riyal.s: The Qatar and Dubai riyal was the currency issued jointly by Qatar and Dubai from 1966 to 1973. It replaced the Gulf rupee after India devalued the rupee in 1966, and was itself replaced by the Qatari riyal in Qatar and by the UAE dirham in Dubai and the other emirates after…

quito.s: Quito is the capital of Ecuador, set in an Andean basin at about 2,850 metres just south of the equator. Centre of local chiefdoms and later the northern capital of the Inca Empire, it was refounded by the Spanish in 1534 and became the seat of the Royal Audiencia of Quito,…

qara-iskander.s: Qara Iskander was ruler of the Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen confederation from 1420, after the death of his father Qara Yusuf. He held Azerbaijan and eastern Anatolia from Tabriz but was repeatedly defeated by the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, who campaigned against him in 1421, 1429 and…

qatif.s: Qatif is an oasis town and port on the Gulf coast of eastern Saudi Arabia, facing the Bahrain islands. Long the main harbour of the al-Ahsa region, it was held in turn by the Qarmatians, Uyunids, Jarwanids and Jabrids, and later by the Ottomans and the Banu Khalid.

qin-er-shi.s: Qin Er Shi, personal name Huhai, was the second emperor of the Qin dynasty, reigning from 210 to 207 BCE. A younger son of Qin Shi Huang, he was placed on the throne by a plot of the eunuch Zhao Gao and the chancellor Li Si, who forged an order for the heir Fusu to kill himself.

qatran-tabrizi.s: Qatran Tabrizi was a Persian poet from Azerbaijan who served local rulers of north-western Iran and the Caucasus, including the Rawwadid emir Abu'l-Hayja Wahsudan and the Shaddadids of Ganja. His odes describe the earthquake that destroyed Tabriz in 1042, and the traveller…

quito-school.s: The Quito School (Escuela Quiteña) was a tradition of painting and sculpture that flourished in Quito during the 17th and 18th centuries. Combining European Baroque models with Andean craftsmanship, its workshops, with artists such as Miguel de Santiago, Bernardo de Legarda…

qudaa.s: Quda'a was a large confederation of Arab tribes whose genealogists disputed whether it belonged to the northern or the southern Arabs. Its tribes, among them Kalb, Tanukh, Salih, Bali and Juhayna, were widespread in the Syrian desert and northern Hejaz in late antiquity, and…

qezel-ozan.s: The Qezel Ozan, the 'red river', is a river of north-western Iran that rises in Kurdistan province and flows through Zanjan province, then joins the Shahrud at Manjil to form the Sefidrud, which cuts through the Alborz mountains to the Caspian Sea. Its valley in Tarom was the…

qavurt.s: Qavurt was a Seljuk prince, son of Chaghri Beg and elder brother of Alp Arslan, who took Kerman in the 1040s and founded the Seljuk dynasty there. He extended his rule to Oman across the Gulf.

qingzhou.s: Qingzhou is a city in central Shandong, China, named after one of the ancient Nine Provinces and an important regional capital from the Han to the Ming. The nearby fortress of Guanggu was the capital of the Southern Yan state from about 400.

qu-yuan.s: Qu Yuan (c. 340–278 BCE) was a poet and minister of the State of Chu, traditionally regarded as the first great individual poet of China. Exiled after his advice to King Huai was rejected, he is credited with the Li Sao and other poems in the Songs of Chu.

quwo-county.s: Quwo County is a county in Linfen, in southern Shanxi province, China. In antiquity Quwo was the base of a junior branch of the ruling house of Jin, which fought the senior line for decades and seized power in 678 BCE under Duke Wu.

qu-wuchen.s: Qu Wuchen, also called Wuchen of Shen, was a noble of the State of Chu who fled to the State of Jin around 589 BCE, taking with him the famous beauty Xia Ji. After Chu destroyed his clan, he went to the State of Wu as an envoy of Jin and taught its people chariot warfare and…

qufu.s: Qufu is a city in south-western Shandong, the capital of the State of Lu in the Zhou period and the birthplace of Confucius. Its Temple of Confucius, the Kong family mansion and the Cemetery of Confucius form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

qungrat.s: The Qungrat are a Turkic tribe of Central Asia, descended from the Mongol Qongirat of the 13th century. Within the Golden Horde and the later Uzbek confederation they were powerful in Khwarazm: the Sufid dynasty of the 14th century sprang from them, and the Qungrat dynasty…

quba.s: Quba is a town in north-eastern Azerbaijan on the slopes of the Greater Caucasus, near the Caspian coast. In the 18th century it was the seat of the Quba Khanate, whose ruler Fatali Khan united much of the eastern Caucasus.

qinnasrin.s: Qinnasrin was an ancient city in northern Syria, south-west of Aleppo, known in Greek and Roman times as Chalcis ad Belum. An important caravan and military town on the desert frontier, it was taken by the Arabs in 637 and became the capital of the military district (jund) of…

qatr-al-nada.s: Qatr al-Nada was the daughter of Khumarawayh, the Tulunid ruler of Egypt. Her marriage to the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tadid, agreed in 892 and celebrated in Baghdad, sealed the peace between the Tulunids and the caliphate.

qalat-jabar.s: Qal'at Ja'bar is a medieval castle on a hill beside the Euphrates in northern Syria, now an island in Lake Assad. Held by the Uqaylid dynasty in the 11th century, it was where the Turkish ruler Zengi was murdered by a servant in 1146 while besieging it.

qirwash-ibn-al-muqallad.s: Qirwash ibn al-Muqallad was the Uqaylid emir of Mosul and the most important ruler of the Arab Uqaylid dynasty, reigning from 1001 to about 1050. He held northern Iraq between the Buyids and the Fatimids, briefly recognising the Fatimid caliph in 1010 before returning to…

quintus-servilius-caepio-consul-106-bce.s: Quintus Servilius Caepio was a Roman general and consul in 106 BCE. He captured Tolosa (Toulouse) from the rebellious Volcae Tectosages and seized its temple treasure, the 'gold of Tolosa', which disappeared on its way to Rome.

qazan-khan-ibn-yasaur.s: Qazan Khan ibn Yasaur was khan of the Chagatai Khanate from about 1343 until his death in 1346 or 1347. He tried to restore the authority of the khan over the tribal amirs of Transoxiana and ruled harshly from his palace near Qarshi.

qifu-clan.s: The Qifu were a Xianbei clan who settled around the upper Yellow River in present-day Gansu in the 3rd and 4th centuries. Their chief Qifu Guoren declared himself ruler in 385 after the collapse of the Former Qin, founding the Western Qin, one of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

qifu-mumo.s: Qifu Mumo was the last ruler of the Western Qin, one of the Sixteen Kingdoms of northern China, reigning from 428 to 431. Pressed by the Northern Liang and Helian Xia, he abandoned his capital and tried to reach the Northern Wei, but he was captured by the Helian Xia, whose…

qiantang-river.s: The Qiantang River is the main river of Zhejiang province in eastern China, flowing past Hangzhou into Hangzhou Bay and the East China Sea. Its funnel-shaped estuary produces the Qiantang tidal bore, one of the largest in the world.

qianling-mausoleum.s: The Qianling Mausoleum is the tomb complex of the Tang emperor Gaozong and his wife Wu Zetian, built into Mount Liang in Qian County, north-west of Xi'an in Shaanxi. Gaozong was buried there in 684 and Wu Zetian in 706.

qarataghliq.s: The Qarataghliq, or 'Black Mountain' faction, was one of two rival branches of the Naqshbandi khojas in Kashgaria, descended from Ishaq Wali, a son of the Sufi master Makhdum-i Azam. Favoured by later khans of Yarkent, they were bitter rivals of the Aqtaghliq ('White…

qingyang.s: Qingyang is a city in the east of Gansu province, China, on the Loess Plateau near the borders of Shaanxi and Ningxia. In ancient times the area was home to the Yiqu, a Rong people who rivalled the state of Qin until Qin destroyed them in the 3rd century BCE.

qiang-historical-people.s: The Qiang were pastoral and farming peoples of north-western China, living in the regions of modern Gansu, Qinghai and western Sichuan. They appear in Shang oracle bones as enemies and sacrificial victims, and fought the Han dynasty in long frontier wars.

qabus-nama.s: The Qabus-nama is a Persian book of advice written in 1082 to 1083 by the Ziyarid prince Keikavus for his son Gilanshah, and named after the author's grandfather, Qabus ibn Vushmgir. In 44 chapters it covers ethics, religion, kingship, warfare, trade, love and everyday conduct.

qasim-amin.s: Qasim Amin was an Egyptian jurist and Islamic modernist, a co-founder of Cairo University and often counted among the Arab world's first feminists. Born in Alexandria, he took a law degree in Egypt and studied at Montpellier in France, and from 1885 served in Egypt's courts.
